training.prepTitle: How to use them for race prep
training.tip1: Practice with gels on long runs 3–4 weeks before your race to train your gut
training.tip2: Replicate your race-day fuelling schedule during training (same timing, same products)
training.tip3: Start with 1 gel per hour and build up to your target race frequency
training.tip4: Never try a new product on race day — always test in training first

gutTraining.intro: {{days}} days to race day. Here's how to train your gut to absorb {{carbs}}g carbs/hour comfortably. GI issues on race day are almost always a training failure, not bad luck.
gutTraining.nauseaTitle: If you feel nausea in training
gutTraining.nauseaBody: Drop one gel and hold that level for two runs before building again. Never race at a carb load you haven't practised.
gutTraining.raceWeekBody: Stick to exactly what you've trained with. No new products. Keep gel timing consistent on your final shakeout run.
gutTraining.noDate: Add your race date to see a personalised gut training protocol.
gutTraining.phase1.title: Baseline — 2 gels per long run
gutTraining.phase1.body: Take 2× {{gelName}} on your next two long runs (60 min+). One at 20 min, one at 45 min. Focus on timing consistency. Note any stomach response in your training log.
gutTraining.phase2.title: Build to {{carbs}}g carbs/hour
gutTraining.phase2.body: Add a gel every 25 min across a 90-min long run. Swap one for your caffeine gel at the 1-hour mark. Your gut is learning to absorb carbohydrates under effort — this is the critical adaptation window.
gutTraining.phase3.title: Race simulation — full protocol
gutTraining.phase3.body: Two long runs at race effort, minimum 2 hours. Full protocol: bar before, gel every 25 min, caffeine at 1h and 2h. Treat these sessions like races. This is where gut training actually happens.
gutTraining.phase4.title: Confidence run — lock the plan
gutTraining.phase4.body: One 90-min run with your exact race protocol. If everything sits well, the plan is locked. No new products or changes after this point.
gutTraining.phase5.title: Taper — maintain, don't experiment
gutTraining.phase5.body: Reduce volume but keep gel timing on shorter runs. Your gut adapts downward too — do not skip fuelling sessions in taper. Arrive at the start line with a trained gut.

sodiumGap.title: Your sodium is {{pct}}% covered
sodiumGap.body: Gels alone rarely cover sodium in long or hot races. Take capsules with water, and keep drinking to thirst.
carbHint.none: No fuelling needed for this distance
warning.carb_rate_short_race: For events <45 min, carb intake is typically unnecessary
warning.carb_rate_high_short: For short races, carb rates >30 g/h increase GI distress risk
warning.sodium_loading_recommendation: Hot or humid race of 4 hours or more: you can pre-load sodium. Studied protocol: about {{ml}} ml of water with about {{salt}} g table salt dissolved in it (about {{mg}} mg sodium; a level teaspoon of salt is about 6 g). Sip it over about an hour, finishing about 45 minutes before the start. Try it in training first. Skip it if you have high blood pressure or kidney problems.
warning.fluid_overhydration_risk: Long race: drinking more than you sweat is the main cause of dangerously low blood sodium, and extra salt does not prevent it. Drink to thirst. If you are gaining weight during the race, drink less.
warning.training_mode_long_race: Gut training mode is for training runs only — carb target has been raised to a minimum safe level for this race duration. Do not use training mode on race day.

note.beforeSwim: Eat ~90 min before start — well before your swim
note.peanutButter: Best in the first half — peanut butter slows absorption
